newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Daiwa trader sentenced for hiding huge losses.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Daiwa trader sentenced for hiding huge losses.

text.p: A former Daiwa Bank Ltd. bond trader was sentenced to four years in prison on Monday for hiding losses of $1.1 billion in unauthorised trades and conspiring with managers to conceal one of the greatest financial losses ever.

Toshihide Iguchi, a Japanese-born bond trader who worked in Daiwa Bank's New York office, pleaded guilty in October 1995, at which time he told a federal judge that senior managers at the Japanese bank lied to the Federal Reserve about his activities.
Iguchi, 45, was also fined $2 million and ordered to pay $570,000 in restitution.

As part of the agreement with prosecutors, Iguchi, who had been senior executive vice president of the bank's New York branch, admitted six counts of misapplication of bank funds, false entries in bank books and records, money laundering and conspiracy. He admitted incurring the trading losses over an 11-year period.
"There is no question that this was a crime of historical dimensions and potentially world shattering implications," said U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan in sentencing Iguchi.
During last year's plea hearing Iguchi not only implied that senior managers had been involved in the cover-up of his losses, but that other traders joined him in the scheme in 1988.

In February 1996, Daiwa pleaded guilty to 16 charges that it covered up Iguchi's trading losses and agreed to pay a $340 million fine. Federal officials said this was a record fine for a financial institution.
Daiwa officials said they learned of Iguchi's activities when he sent the bank's president a 30-page confession on July 13, 1995. However, the bank did not inform U.S. officials for six weeks.

Iguchi explained in the letter that he had incurred the $1.1 billion loss and concealed it by selling securities without approval from Daiwa's own account or customers' accounts and then forging documents to make the trades look like authorised transactions.
Daiwa officials had said they were shocked by the disclosure and that Iguchi had fooled their auditors for years through 30,000 forged trading slips.

Even after the bank's president received Iguchi's letter, prosecutors alleged that Daiwa falsely informed the Federal Reserve Board in a quarterly report filed on July 31, 1995 that it still held $600 million in U.S. Treasury obligations that Iguchi had earlier sold to cover his trading losses.
Iguchi told the judge that senior managers also told him to continue the scheme until at least September. He said he kept selling securities and continued to falsify bank records to conceal the loss.

He also told the judge that senior managers of Daiwa's New York branch conspired in 1993 to lie to the Federal Reserve Board about Iguchi's supervision of the branch's trading department and its trading activities.

Prosecutors alleged that whenever Iguchi lost money as a government bond trader, he took bonds without approval from Daiwa's own account or those of its customers, sold them, and then forged documents to make the trades look like authorised transactions.
Masahiro Tsuda, former general manager of Daiwa's New York branch, also pleaded guilty to his role in the scandal and was sentenced in October to two months in prison and fined $100,000.
